newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia remembers Lenin with tributes and promises.
newsitem.headline: Russia remembers Lenin with tributes and promises.

text.p: Thousands filed past the embalmed body of Vladimir Lenin on Tuesday on the anniversary of his birth but some seemed more motivated by a communist-style promise of free housing for political loyalty.
Many in the overwhelmingly elderly crowd were true believers, carrying red roses and banners, and were ready to recite the old Soviet slogans at the slightest prompting.
"I'm here to honor the birthday of our great leader of the Soviet Communist Party Vladimir Ilich Lenin," said unemployed factory worker Igor Fyodorov.
But many came to prove their loyalty to a pro-communist organisation that promises Moscow apartments for those who pay just a million roubles ($175).

After walking through Lenin's mausoleum these hopefuls formed long lines in another throwback to Soviet times. This time the goal was not cheap sausage, but a register recording the names of those who had faithfully attended Tuesday's celebration.
"We're trying to set up a communist-style system," said Kima Gurskaya, an official at the Youth Housing Cooperative. "We're trying to find work and housing for people."
Saying 370 people had already received apartments, she denied the plan was another variant of the pyramid schemes that have flourished in Russia since the 1991 collapse of communism.

Inside Lenin's mausoleum on Red Square next to the red-bricked Kremlin walls, stern-faced guards enforced rules dating back to Soviet times. "Get your hands out of your pockets," they ordered visitors. "Men, take off your hats."

Because of the frailty of many visitors the guards eased up on the usual demand that all entering the darkened tomb walk past the body at a brisk pace. Some shuffled cautiously ahead, wiping away tears as they approached the hallowed place.
Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov led the faithful in laying flowers at the mausoleum, although a few youths tried unsuccessfully to lob tomatoes at him before he arrived on Red Square.

Others used the occasion to lay flowers at other tombs of Soviet dignitaries behind Lenin's mausoleum. Soviet dictator Joseph Stalin's grave overflowed with fresh roses. Just a few plastic flowers covered longtime leader Leonid Brezhnev's grave.
The crowd was nearly unanimous in their opinion that Lenin's body -- which still receives regular infusions of chemicals to give it a human appearance -- should not be buried.
"Our forefathers decided not to bury him and we should maintain this tradition," said Sergei Soyuzov, 75, a plumber honoured with the Soviet-era title "Hero of Socialist Labour".
Maj. Gen. Alexei Grigoriyevich, who declined to give his last name, said: "I served the Soviet army 43 years and I am ready to serve again. We won't give up Lenin!"
Vladimir Yurchik, 69, a retired engineer cited the precedent of Russian pioneering surgeon Nikolai Pirogov, who has been embalmed in the Ukraine for more than a century.
President Boris Yeltsin last month again raised the possibility of burying Lenin, whose preservation is now funded by private contributions, and floated the idea of a referendum on the issue.
Russia's communist-led parliament reacted angrily, passing a resolution aimed at blocking any effort to bury the Bolshevik leader.
